channel.title: KV Cache
channel.description: Paper reviews on shrinking, evicting and reusing the KV cache: compression, quantization, eviction signals, offloading and prefix reuse.

item.title: LoopVQ: Sub 1-bit KV Cache Quantization for Looped Transformers
item.description:
Paper

Introduction

A looped transformer is a model that reuses the same group of layers several times. It saves parameters, but each iteration step has to keep its own key/value cache, so the serving bottleneck shifts from the weights to the cache. This post summarizes the observations, design, and measured results of LoopVQ, a method that compresses that cache to under 1 bit per element.

item.title: SpecOPD: Branch-Parallel On-Policy Distillation for Speculative Decoding
item.description:
Paper

SpecOPD: Training Speculative Decoding Drafters with Branch Parallelism

Introduction

Speculative decoding speeds up generation by having a small drafter propose multiple tokens that a large target verifies in a single pass. But the ceiling on that speed is set by how many tokens the drafter can get right in a row, and on-policy distillation, the approach aimed at this problem, is tied to sequential draft-verify rollouts while collecting its training signal. SpecOPD starts from the observation that this sequential dependence is not essential to on-policy learning.

item.title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention
item.description:
Paper

Introduction

As context grows longer, softmax attention’s compute grows quadratically with context length, and the key-value cache grows proportionally to context length. Linear attention, which avoids this, compresses context into a fixed-size matrix memory, but the problem remained that editing that memory disturbs other memories already stored. This paper proposes the Kronecker delta rule, which narrows the scope touched by a single update, and KronLSTM, which implements it as gates.

item.title: TAO: Tool-Aware Joint Scheduling for LLM-Based Agentic Serving
item.description:
Paper

TAO: Tool-Aware Joint Scheduling for LLM-Based Agentic Serving

Original: Shuhuai Li et al., “TAO: Tool-Aware Joint Scheduling for LLM-Based Agentic Serving” (arXiv:2610.37230v1, preprint). The following account is based solely on the attached original text.

Introduction

Agents alternate between model inference and external tool execution. While a tool runs, that session’s GPU demand becomes suspendable; how this gap is used and which node the session is attached to when it returns determine response time. This paper proposes TAO, a framework that binds both problems into a single scheduling problem.

item.title: On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction
item.description:
Paper

Diffusion language models must decide ‘what’ and ‘where’ at the same time

Diffusion language models generate sentences by repeatedly filling masked tokens. To decode exactly, each model forward must commit only the single most certain masked position as a token, which is slow; committing multiple positions at once to increase speed degrades generation quality. This paper moves speculative decoding, a lossless acceleration technique validated on autoregressive models, to diffusion language models, but finds the solution by predicting not tokens but the order of which position to fill next.

item.title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization
item.description: Paper Recent language models keep increasing the amount of information packed into a single vocabulary entry. Per-layer embeddings (PLE), first introduced in Gemma 3n, carried over to Gemma 4: instead of a single input-layer vector per vocabulary item, each decoder layer has a different learned vector. This post examines OPTIC, which shrinks this table by about 100× while retaining most of the original performance, starting from the problem setting and proceeding through a small example, the method, results, and limitations.

item.title: Intern Lumina U2: A Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation
item.description:
Paper

Problem: Why It’s Hard to Unify Understanding and Generation in One Representation

There have been many attempts to merge image understanding and image generation into a single model. Most, however, optimize the two abilities separately in different representation spaces. When text is trained as a token classification problem and images are trained with a diffusion/flow objective over continuous vectors, the two objectives push against each other within one backbone, which tends to make training unstable.

item.title: Cache Engineering for Agents
item.description:
Paper

The Cost and Accuracy Dilemma of Long Agent Trajectories

LLM agents accumulate long trajectories by repeating reasoning and tool calls for hundreds of rounds. To make inference fast, the already-computed key-value (KV) cache must stay on the GPU and be read again for each next token; as the trajectory grows, storage and read costs increase. The paper measures KV cache reads at 82.4% of total API cost (§1, Figure 13), and points out that accuracy degrades once the number of KVs or the positional span handled by attention exceeds what the model can handle (§1).

item.title: DLite: History-free Speculative Decoding for Agentic AI
item.description:
As a coding agent reads files and calls tools, its conversation and execution history grows. Adding a small model to draft answers faster can create another burden if that model must separately process and retain the same long history.

DLite lets the target model handle the history, while the small drafter uses the target’s internal representations to propose upcoming tokens. It removes the drafter’s separate historical KV cache. It does not remove the target’s cache or discard historical information.

item.title: HLA-WM: Hybrid Linear Attention for Long-Horizon Video World Models
item.description:
Paper

arXiv:2610.05739 · Monash University · The University of Adelaide · Zhejiang University

One-Line Summary (TL;DR)

Recurrent linear attention (Gated DeltaNet) in video world models compresses memory into a fixed-size state, which is efficient, but when the camera leaves and returns, distant scenes are progressively forgotten. HLA-WM caches chunk-level affine summaries in a training-free way and uses camera geometry (frustum overlap) to retrieve and recompose the relevant scenes, achieving PSNR +0.74 dB, rotation error −28.5%, and a 12× reduction versus Full KV in history memory over a 60-second rollout (about 6× the memory of GDN) (source: §Abstract, Fig. 1).

item.title: Towards Looped Models Done Right, Part II: Rethinking at Fixed Points
item.description:
Paper

TL;DR

In looped language models, the state converges to a fixed point $z^\star = F_\theta(z^\star; x)$ as the recursion depth grows, and near the fixed point the “endpoint” can stand in for the entire trajectory. This paper uses that one property to reduce four different costs at once across pretraining, serving, and RL: (1) training backpropagates only through the last $b$ recursions (truncated BPTT), (2) decoding caches only the last KV bank for each token (terminal KV sharing, a $3\times$ cut in cache), (3) prefill is distilled into a lightweight student that predicts the fixed point directly, giving up to a $1.79\times$ speedup, and (4) RL reuses gradients from stored rollout states to make updates $2\times$ faster. It also improves the two devices that actually produce this fixed point — the depth prior and input injection — as a “learned prior” and “orthogonal injection (OrthoInj)” respectively, lowering perplexity across the whole range from 100M to 1.6B parameters (source: §1).

item.title: TRACE: Rollout-Guided Quantization-Aware Training for FP4 Reinforcement Learning of MoE Language Models
item.description:
Paper

TRACE: Rollout-Aligned FP4 Quantization-Aware Training — MoE LLM RL at BF16 Quality, up to 5.4x Faster

TL;DR

In reinforcement learning (RL) for MoE LLMs, quantizing rollout generation to FP4 (W4A4 + FP4 KV) speeds up generation by up to 5.4x, but it widens the numerical mismatch between the training path and the rollout path, making training unstable or causing collapse. This paper proposes TRACE, which uses the FP4 quantization results actually produced on the rollout side directly as a signal to steer the rounding decisions on the training side, preserving nearly identical performance to BF16 rollouts while capturing FP4’s speed advantage (source: §1, §0).

item.title: SlimKV: Joint Token-Feature KV Cache Compression with Reconstruction-Free Beacon Attention
item.description:
Paper

SlimKV: Compressing Tokens and Features Together, Cutting the KV Cache by up to 32× with Reconstruction-Free Latent-Space Attention

TL;DR

SlimKV is a question-agnostic framework that compresses the KV cache — the bottleneck of long-context LLM inference — simultaneously along the token axis and the feature axis. The key idea is to remove RoPE only from the Keys of beacon memory tokens, so attention is performed directly in the latent space without a reconstruction step. It achieves the best performance at 16×/32× compression on LongBench (source: §5.2), and at a 128K token length it delivers up to 7.34× attention speedup and 3.38× end-to-end decoding speedup over no compression (source: §5.4).

item.title: Tailoring the Quantization Space for 1-Bit KV Cache Compression
item.description:
Paper

TaSQ: ‘Tailored Design’ of the Quantization Space for a 1-bit KV Cache

TL;DR — TaSQ (Tailored Space Vector Quantization) redesigns the very target space to which vector quantization (VQ) is applied, compressing the KV cache to about 1.25 bits per channel while maintaining quality close to BF16. The key is applying query-guided channel weighting, head-shared normalization, and covariance-aware channel grouping to the pre-RoPE key. On a single RTX 6000 Ada, it expands the KV cache pool by 12.48× and raises the maximum batch from 6→84 (14×) and peak throughput by 1.87× (source: §Abstract, Fig. 4).

item.title: Prefill-Free Cross-Family KV Cache Transfer for Heterogeneous Multi-Agent LLMs
item.description:
Paper

How to Hand Off KV Caches As-Is Between Different LLMs: HeteroFold

TL;DR: HeteroFold, a method that reuses the KV cache between models with different tokenizers and architectures without the receiver re-prefilling, beats existing cache transfer in all six directions and is 10.74× faster than native prefill at 32K context (source: §4.1, Tab.1, Tab.4).

item.title: The KV Cache Is the New Memory Wall
item.description:
Paper

The KV Cache Is the New Memory Wall: Three Regimes and Five Domains of Long-Context LLM Inference

TL;DR — Long-context LLM decode inference is bound by memory bandwidth, not arithmetic, and once context length crosses a specific computable “crossover” point, the bottleneck shifts from model weights to the KV cache. This paper unifies the five families of techniques that aim to reduce the KV cache (quantization, token eviction, paging, prefix caching, tiering) into a single footprint model, derives exact crossover context lengths and speedup ceilings on roofline maps of the H100/B200/MI300X, and realigns results that were measured in different settings and could not be compared onto a single coordinate system.

item.title: WavePP: High-Throughput Pipeline Parallel LLM Prefill under Prefix Reuse
item.description:
Paper

WavePP — A Pipeline-Parallel Prefill Runtime That Burns In Prefix Reuse

TL;DR

Built on top of TensorRT-LLM, WavePP overlaps request admission (reuse consensus, cache protection, capacity reservation) asynchronously with pipeline execution, and dynamically tunes the wave size to keep the pipeline full. On the same kernels and the same topology, it pushed prefill throughput for GLM 5.2 and MiniMax M2.7 up to 2.91×/2.02×, and across the 28 Kimi K3 settings it recorded the highest throughput in all 18 with concurrency 8 or higher.

item.title: Periodic Weak Spots: Phase Sensitivity from Chunked KV-Cache Compression
item.description:
Paper

Phase Sensitivity: The ‘Periodic Weakness’ Created by Chunked KV-Cache Compression

TL;DR — In models that use chunked KV-cache compression (such as the DeepSeek-V4 family), the same information can vary in retrieval performance by up to 40pp periodically depending on its ‘phase’ relative to the compression window boundary. Average benchmark scores completely hide this weakness.

item.title: WorldAttention: An Efficient Attention Architecture for Interactive Video World Models
item.description:
Paper

WorldAttention: System Co-Design of an Interactive Video World Model That Drops the Sliding Window

TL;DR — Text-controlled interactive video world models are trapped between the demand to “remember the entire history” and the reality that “the KV cache grows linearly until GPU memory blows up.” Researchers at Alibaba DAMO Academy solve this dilemma with an attention architecture called WorldAttention. A hierarchical KV cache (HKV) splits memory into pages and distributes them across a multi-tier memory hierarchy, a hybrid sparse attention (HSA) makes the computation linear and sparse, and custom kernels push actual hardware performance to the limit. The results are a VBench-Long subject consistency of 0.9472, an InterVBench score of 0.9668, and 22.0 FPS on a single H100 GPU (source: Abstract, Tab. 1).

item.title: Block Sparse Attention with Log-Linear Complexity
item.description:
Paper

PISA: Pyramid Top-$K$ Selection Lowers the Cost of Block-Sparse Attention to $O(N\log N)$

TL;DR — Block-sparse attention makes attention computation linear, but block selection still costs quadratic time. PISA solves this by layering keys into a pyramid via average pooling and narrowing candidates at each level with LogSumExp (LSE) scores. Prefill selection cost drops to $O(N\log N)$ and decode to $O(\log N)$, delivering up to $9.95\times$ speedup in selection latency over existing BSA at 256K tokens.

item.title: Who Pays for the KV Cache? Attributing Shared AI Inference Spend Across Kubernetes and LLM Provider Bills
item.description:
Paper

Who pays for the KV cache? — Kubernetes, gateway, and provider bills in one ledger

TL;DR — The cost of a single AI feature is scattered across three disconnected ledgers: Kubernetes allocations, gateway logs, and provider per-token bills. The authors build unalloc, an open-source tool that merges these three ledgers into a single Decimal-exact ledger, and ask “how much spend belongs to no one at all (unowned spend)?” The conclusion is sobering: within the same inference server, a given tenant’s billing share varies by up to 13.7 pp depending on which meter (tokens vs. time vs. KV memory) you use, and if you attach labels only to the leader pod, 66% of monthly GPU cost is left without an owner (source: §4, §6, §9).

item.title: GDN Tree-Scan: Served Tree Verification for Recurrent-Hybrid Language Models
item.description:
Paper

LumoTree: Path-Parallel Speculative Verification for Hybrid Language Models

TL;DR — Tree speculative decoding in hybrid models that mix Gated DeltaNet with full attention requires three things to line up on the same “accepted path”: the recurrent state, the convolution history, and the attention KV cache. LumoTree coordinates verification and commit through a single shared tree descriptor, and implements this with a path-parallel scan plus native replay. On an NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10), it verifies a 27-candidate tree at a cost comparable to a chain stack, and records +7.7%–+11.8% decode throughput over chain MTP. The authors themselves make clear, however, that it does not speed up task completion.

item.title: Adapting Tree-Structured Speculative Decoding to DeepSeek-V4 for Efficient Inference
item.description:
Paper

Branching on Compressed Memory: Adding Tree Reasoning to DeepSeek-V4

TL;DR Adding tree-structured speculative decoding to DeepSeek-V4-Flash yields longer acceptance length and up to about 18.5% higher decode throughput under the same verification budget (source: §5, Fig. 4). The key is not the tree itself, but the verification-side adaptation that isolates compressed attention state per branch and commits only the accepted path (source: §4).

item.title: Flash-dLLM: IO-Aware KV Caching and Parallel Decoding for Fast, Memory-Efficient Diffusion LLMs
item.description:
Paper

Flash-dLLM: I/O-First Diffusion LLM Acceleration, Unlocking 210.6 tokens/s with Fused Cache and Self-Verification

One-Line Summary (TL;DR)

Diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) support parallel denoising, but combining KV cache reuse with parallel decoding makes GPU memory I/O the bottleneck (source: §1). Flash-dLLM combines Flash-Cache, which fuses QKV projection, RoPE, and cache writes in SRAM with no training, and Flash-Verify, in which the dLLM itself serves as both drafter and verifier, achieving 210.6 tokens/s on GSM8K-512 with LLaDA-1.5, an 81.0× speedup, and 5.1× and 11.0× speedups over Elastic-Cache (source: Tab. 1, Tab. 2, Abstract).

item.title: H-Spec: Parallel Speculative Decoding Without a Drafter-Side KV Cache
item.description:
Paper

Parallel Inference without Drafter-Side KV Cache: H-Spec’s Hybrid Speculative Decoding

TL;DR shows that the bottleneck in concurrent serving is that a block-diffusion drafter must project target hidden states at every token to maintain a separate KV cache, and combines in-place target KV reuse with $O(1)$ injection of the last-token hidden state in a Mamba-attention hybrid to eliminate the cache while raising mean accepted length and throughput together (source: §1, §3.2, Tab. 2, Fig. 6).

item.title: Analytical Power-Aware Provisioning for Prefill-Decode Disaggregated AI Inference
item.description:
Paper

How Many Prefills and How Many Decodes Within a Power Budget: The Capacity-Power Pareto Front for PD-Disaggregated Inference

One-Line Summary (TL;DR)

This paper derives closed-form expressions for how provisioning $(n_P, n_D)$ in prefill-decode disaggregated inference determines serving capacity $\mu$ (req/s) and average power $P$ (W), and shows how to select the minimum-power configuration on the capacity-power Pareto front over candidate deployments (source: §2.2, §2.3). The key is modeling the coupling in which decode-side KV cache is shared between active decode requests and reservations for requests waiting for and running prefill, as a memory balance (source: §3.1.3, Fig. 2). Serving Qwen3-32B (32.8B params) on H200 GPUs (peak 989 TFLOP/s, 4.8 TB/s) with SGLang 0.5.9, the experiments achieve capacity errors of 1.2% (fixed length, 4096 input tokens / 256 output tokens), 3.0% (Mooncake trace), and 1.6% (Azure trace), and power errors of 2.3%, 2.7%, and 2.6% (source: §5.2, Tab. 2, Tab. 3).

item.title: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: Pushing the Limits of KV Cache Compression
item.description:
Paper

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: A Multimodal MoE That Cuts the KV Cache to 1/4 While Raising Performance Further

TL;DR. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, released by DeepSeek-AI, is a multimodal MoE with a 552B backbone that supports up to a 1M token context. It combines Causal Encoder-Decoder (CED), Compressed Sparse Attention 2 (CSA2), FP4 KV cache, and SWA Bounded Replay to cut the global KV cache to 890 bytes per token (about 1/4 of the predecessor DeepSeek-V4-Flash) and the persistent KV cache to about 1/8 (source: Abstract, §6). Even so, it stands shoulder to shoulder with closed frontier models on agent benchmarks, including DeepSWE v1.1 74.2% and Terminal-Bench 2.1 90.6% (source: Table 3, §5.3.2).

item.title: Fathom: Per-Query Read Depth for Sparse Decoding over Offloaded KV Caches
item.description:
Paper

Fathom: Accelerating 1M-Token Decoding by 1.67x with Query-Adaptive Depth Scanning

TL;DR

When agent sessions stretch to 1M tokens and dozens of sessions reside concurrently, the KV cache and the index used to rank it must live in host memory, making the top-k scan at every decode step bound by PCIe bytes (source: §1). Fathom stores the 4-bit K cache as channel-major bit-planes so that reading the leading $t$ planes yields an exact $t$-bit quantization, and each query partitions its bit budget across channels via reverse water-filling based on per-channel importance $g_j$ (source: §3.2, §3.3). On Qwen3-8B at 1M tokens with batch size 1, it is 1.67x faster in GPU time than a 136-bit scan, 2.50x faster than landmarks, and 3.12x faster than thumbnails, while achieving 1.1–5.3x lower attention error with 18% fewer bytes than SparQ r=16 at matched GPU time (source: Tab. 1, Tab. 2, Tab. 5). However, it provides no speedup when the index resides in HBM (source: §7).

item.title: ZGCM-1: A Fully Open and Extremely Efficient Foundation Model for Math and Agentic Search
item.description:
Paper

ZGCM-1: How a 7B Dense Model Trades Blows with 235B Frontiers — A Fully Open, Ultra-Efficient Foundation Model Design Report

TL;DR — With a single 7.39B dense model, ZGCM-1 scores 75.0% on AIME 2026, 63.1% on WebWalkerQA, and 62.0% on Binary Function Search, breaking the conventional wisdom that “frontier reasoning is the exclusive province of tens of billions of parameters.” The secret is not inflating parameters but a fully open recipe built on a hybrid architecture of gated sliding-window attention + global attention that cuts the KV cache by 6.4×, FP8 + Muon + TWEO that shortens pretraining by roughly 4.2×, and MDP mid-training that learns 256K long contexts.

item.title: SAS: Simple Attention Sparsification via End-to-End Optimization of Context Ranking
item.description:
Paper

SAS: A Simple Attention Sparsification That Learns Context Ranking Directly Without Distillation

TL;DR — In post-training attention sparsification, inject the continuous scores produced by the selector into the attention logits as a log gate. This bypasses the gradients blocked by discrete Top-K selection, allowing the selector to be trained end-to-end with the language modeling loss, without auxiliary distillation. As a result, at a tight budget (1024 tokens), it lifts GPQA-Diamond by up to +15.5 points over SeerAttention-R on Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, and cuts decoding latency by up to 5.6× at 512K context.
